speaker: Tim Latimer
title: Tim Latimer on Solving the Financing Problem for Geothermal
question: Why does permitting a geothermal power project in the western United States typically take years longer than permitting comparable oil and gas drilling?
guest: Through a quirk of history, the best geology for geothermal is located in the western United States, which is predominantly owned by the US federal government rather than private landowners. That puts us by default into a federal permitting regime on pretty much every project in a way that isn't true of other energy resources, so we've had to go through multi-year NEPA approval processes alongside transmission and interconnection. We need the right environmental standards, but there are redundant steps and offices that aren't staffed well, so typical permitting for a western geothermal project takes about six to eight years. One of the funny things is that even though we're drilling wells just like oil and gas, we haven't benefited from the same permitting. For early exploration or routine extensions to existing projects, oil and gas has legislatively developed categorical exclusions from full environmental reviews. The law passed in 2005 didn't say drilling—it specifically said oil and gas drilling. That's been interpreted to exclude geothermal, so even though geothermal is a lower-impact, zero-emission resource, it faces a much more extensive permitting program on federal land.

models.answer:
The main reason is that geothermal projects on federal land, where most of the best western resources sit, have historically had to pass through environmental review under the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) several separate times, while oil and gas drilling gets statutory shortcuts.

A geothermal developer typically faces separate reviews at the land-use planning and leasing stage, then for exploration, then for drilling wells, and again for building the power plant and transmission lines. Each can require an environmental assessment or a full impact statement, which adds up to as many as six reviews and often seven to ten years in total.

Oil and gas, by contrast, received categorical exclusions under Section 390 of the Energy Policy Act of 2005, letting many wells on already-leased or previously disturbed land skip detailed review. Geothermal was left out, despite similar drilling techniques and surface footprints.

Other factors compound this: understaffed Bureau of Land Management offices with little geothermal expertise, irregular lease sales, and litigation risk.

Recent reforms, including new BLM categorical exclusions for geothermal exploration and emergency permitting procedures, have begun to narrow the gap.

models.answer: Permitting a western U.S. geothermal project typically takes seven to ten years, far longer than comparable oil and gas drilling, due to land ownership, unequal environmental laws, and broader infrastructure needs. Roughly 90 percent of western geothermal resources lie beneath federal lands managed by the Bureau of Land Management and U.S. Forest Service, whereas most U.S. oil and gas wells are drilled on private or state land under faster state-level rules. Even on federal land, the Energy Policy Act of 2005 granted oil and gas broad statutory categorical exclusions that bypass lengthy National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) reviews. Despite recent administrative exclusions for early exploration, geothermal lacks statutory parity and can trigger up to six sequential NEPA reviews covering land-use planning, leasing, exploration, wellfield drilling, power plant construction, and transmission. Finally, unlike oil that can be piped or trucked away, geothermal heat must be converted to electricity on-site, requiring power-plant and grid-interconnection permits alongside drilling approvals from federal field offices with infrequent lease sales and far fewer dedicated geothermal staff.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
The main reason is the law. Most western geothermal resources are on federal land managed by the Bureau of Land Management, and federal rules treat geothermal differently from oil and gas even though both involve drilling wells. Since the Energy Policy Act of 2005 (Section 390), oil and gas operators have been able to use "categorical exclusions." These let many wells, especially in areas that already have an approved plan or recent drilling, skip a full environmental review under NEPA (the National Environmental Policy Act). Geothermal got no such exemption.

As a result, a geothermal project often needs a separate NEPA review at each stage: leasing, exploration, drilling test wells, and then building the plant. Each review can take one to two years and can be challenged in court. Developers also can't know whether a site has enough heat and flow until they drill, so they may go through all these reviews and find nothing usable. Add tribal consultation, endangered species reviews, water rights, and connecting to the grid, and geothermal timelines often reach seven to ten years, compared with months for many oil and gas permits.

Recent federal moves, including new categorical exclusions for geothermal exploration, have started to close the gap. They don't cover every stage yet.

noweb.answer: Most high-grade geothermal resources in the western United States sit beneath federal lands managed by the Bureau of Land Management or the Forest Service, triggering National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) reviews. Unlike oil and gas development, which gained broad statutory categorical exclusions under the Energy Policy Act of 2005 to bypass lengthy NEPA analyses for routine exploration and drilling, geothermal projects have historically lacked comparable statutory exemptions. Consequently, geothermal developers often face multiple sequential environmental reviews across leasing, exploratory drilling, field development, power plant construction, and transmission, with even low-impact test wells requiring months- or year-long assessments. By contrast, oil and gas permitting benefits from standardized procedures, dedicated agency staffing, and far more activity on private or state lands exempt from federal NEPA review. Finally, geothermal projects must also permit an on-site power plant and grid interconnection, whereas oil and gas wells can typically tie into existing pipelines.
